313:- SSHes to `<ssh-target>`, detects the remote platform, and **auto-installs a matching herdr server binary there** — the remote does **not** need herdr pre-installed (it does need SSH access + permission to install/run a binary).
314:- Bridges your **local clipboard** (including image paste) to the remote server and keeps your **local keybindings** (`--remote-keybindings server` to use the server's instead).
315:- `--session NAME` picks/creates a named session on the remote; `--handoff` opts into live handoff.
317:**Config** — the `[remote]` block in `config.toml`:
320:- `remote_image_paste` (`[keys]`) — raw-key image-paste binding, active only under `--remote`.
322:**Troubleshooting `remote platform detection failed: Connection closed by <host> port 22`**: this is a **transient SSH-level close**, not a herdr config problem. Verify the SSH path herdr uses actually works, then just retry:
328:If plain SSH works, retry `herdr --remote <ssh-target>`; if it keeps failing, check `~/.config/herdr/herdr-client.log` / `herdr.log` right after the failure. Common real causes: SSH auth needing an interactive prompt the bridge can't answer, or sshd rate-limiting rapid connections (`MaxStartups`).
330:## Running herdr nested inside tmux (multi-remote)
332:The repo's default stance is herdr **or** tmux, not nested. But you can deliberately nest — tmux as the outer window manager with several inner herdr clients, some local and some `herdr --remote <host>` to different servers. The catch is the **prefix collision**: both default to `Ctrl+b`, so outer tmux swallows it and inner herdr never sees its prefix ([herdr #759](https://github.com/ogulcancelik/herdr/discussions/759)).
338:3. **Don't nest — use herdr's native remoting.** `herdr --remote <target> [--remote-keybindings local|server]` runs a local thin client against a remote herdr server without tmux in the middle, and herdr hosts multiple named sessions itself. For a pure "multiple remotes" need this is often cleaner than nesting; `--remote-keybindings local` (default) keeps your local keymap, `server` uses the remote's.
383:**It cannot be a herdr-plus Quick Action** (`prefix + y`), which is the intuitive place to look. Two blockers: Quick Actions run through `sh -c` with **no PTY/stdin** — the same reason `btop`/`nvtop` are command panes rather than Quick Actions — and every action is a fixed `command = "…"` string with no free-text field.
396:> **Why `Alt+Enter` had to exist.** Plain Enter cannot express *"run exactly what I typed"* while fzf still has a match — type `ls -la` with `ls -la /tmp` in history and Enter takes the history entry, which makes the picker feel like it can only replay old commands. `--expect=alt-enter` adds the escape hatch. Note that fzf's line layout is **not fixed**: with `--print-query --expect`, a no-match Enter prints only the query (one line), while an accepted match prints query / key / selection. The helper therefore reads the key from line 2 (empty or absent ⇒ plain Enter) and only trusts line 3 on exit code 0.
398:## Copy pane + space facts to the clipboard {#copy-to-clipboard}
400:Six one-keypress "grab this onto the clipboard" ops, all driven by one helper (`~/.config/herdr/pane-copy.sh` = [`dot_config/herdr/executable_pane-copy.sh`](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles/blob/main/dot_config/herdr/executable_pane-copy.sh)). It distills a herdr CLI call into human-readable text and pipes it to the repo's own [`x copy`](../shells/aliases.md) (auto-selects pbcopy / wl-copy / xclip / xsel / OSC 52; `x` is resolved by absolute-path fallback since a command-pane may run without the interactive PATH). The pane defaults to the **current focused pane** (`herdr pane current`); the keybinds pass `$HERDR_ACTIVE_PANE_ID`, the Quick Actions pass `$HERDR_PLUS_PANE_ID`, and either falls through to the current-pane lookup when empty.
402:| Op | Key | Quick Action | What lands on the clipboard |
413:Both surfaces share the same helper: the `[[keys.command]]` binds in [`.chezmoitemplates/herdr/config.toml`](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles/blob/main/.chezmoitemplates/herdr/config.toml) and the `copy-*.toml` **Quick Actions** under `dot_config/herdr/plugins/config/cloudmanic.herdr-plus/quick-actions/` (fuzzy-launched via `prefix+y`). `P/D/V/S` are uppercase (`prefix+shift+<letter>`) chosen to dodge herdr's reserved `shift+H/J/K/L` (swap-pane) and this repo's `shift+B` (new_worktree) / `shift+R` (reload); lowercase `d` was the only free mnemonic letter left for the dir ops, with `ctrl+d` keeping the pair adjacent. Confirm no collision with `herdr server reload-config` (empty `diagnostics`).
445:| Patterns | `http(s)` / `ftp` / `file`, bare `www.` → `http://`, `IPv4[:port]` → `http://`, `git@…` SSH remotes → `https://…`, quoted `"owner/repo"` → `github.com/owner/repo`, `import "pkg"` → `npmjs.com/package/pkg` |
453:The copy-path sibling of the URL picker. `prefix+p` opens an fzf popup of the file paths in the focused pane; pick one (or several) and the path is copied to the clipboard. Lowercase `p` ("copy **p**ath") sits under the uppercase copy family (`prefix+P/D/V/S`), the same `u`/`U` convention. On tmux the analog is the **extrakto** plugin (`prefix + Tab`) — see [tmux keybindings](tmux/keybindings.md).
463:| **Two-tier list** | Paths that **exist** show first (copied as their resolved **absolute** path); everything else — remote / stale / hypothetical — appears below a `── unverified ──` separator (still selectable), so real-but-unresolvable paths aren't lost |
465:`path:line:col` suffixes (grep `-n` / stack traces / compiler output) are stripped before the existence test, so `pkg.py:42:5` validates as `pkg.py`. Scope is the visible screen by default (`--source recent` for scrollback); multi-select copies newline-joined; an empty result prints `no file paths found` and pauses ~1.5 s.
474:- **OSC133 copy-mode** (`cpout` / `cpblock`, prompt-jump, last-output yank) is tmux-specific. herdr's copy mode (`prefix+[`) is vi-style but has no OSC133 prompt-boundary awareness. `cpcmd` (zsh history, multiplexer-agnostic) still works.
```

   200	    # NSPasteboardItem.string(forType:) directly and get nil. writeObjects

     1	#!/usr/bin/env sh
     2	# ~/.config/herdr/pane-copy.sh
     3	# Source: dot_config/herdr/executable_pane-copy.sh (managed by chezmoi)
     4	#
     5	# Copy distilled facts about a herdr pane to the system clipboard. Five targets:
     6	#
     7	#   process  the foreground processes running in the pane (cmdline + pid + cwd)
     8	#   coord    the pane's coordinate in herdr's Session > Workspace > Tab > Pane
     9	#            hierarchy, in a paste-ready form (the ids the herdr CLI accepts, plus
    10	#            the socket path that selects a non-default session — there is NO
    11	#            --session flag on the pane/tab/workspace subcommands)
    12	#   content  the pane's terminal content — visible screen (--source visible) or
    13	#            the full retained scrollback (--source recent, the default)
    14	#   dir      the WORKSPACE ("space") root directory — what the sidebar row you
    15	#            would right-click represents: the cwd of the space's OLDEST tab.
    16	#            Derived by space-root.sh (herdr has no workspace-level cwd field);
    17	#            read the caveat there about the sidebar label drifting from it.
    18	#   cwd      the pane's LIVE working directory — the `abspath`/`pwd` answer,
    19	#            which drifts away from `dir` the moment you cd.
    20	#
    21	# The pane defaults to the CURRENT focused pane (`herdr pane current`); pass a
    22	# pane id to target another. herdr's keybind context passes $HERDR_ACTIVE_PANE_ID
    23	# and herdr-plus Quick Actions pass $HERDR_PLUS_PANE_ID — both are wired to call
    24	# this, and both fall through to the current-pane lookup when empty.

    26	# Clipboard sink is the repo's own `x copy` (dot_dotfiles/bin/executable_x), which
    27	# auto-selects pbcopy / wl-copy / xclip / xsel / OSC 52. We resolve it by absolute
    28	# path fallback because a herdr command-pane / quick-action pane may run us via
    29	# `sh -c` without the interactive-shell PATH.
    30	#
    31	# Usage:
    32	#   pane-copy.sh process [PANE_ID]
    33	#   pane-copy.sh coord   [PANE_ID]
    34	#   pane-copy.sh content [PANE_ID] [--source visible|recent]

The command runs where the Unix socket is accessible. 127:| Search all pane content + jump | **CLI pipeline + fzf + exact-focus helper** | `prefix+Alt+F` → `herdr-grep --pick --visible`; Alt+S searches unwrapped scrollback |

161:| `` prefix + u `` | **URL picker** — fzf-pick a URL from the pane and open it (`x open`); tmux-fzf-url analog. `--source recent` = full scrollback | command pane |
165:| `prefix + Alt + F` | prompt for pane-content pattern → `herdr-grep --pick --visible` → fzf exact jump; Alt+S = scrollback, Alt+V = visible | command pane |
171:| `prefix + S` | copy focused pane's **content** (full scrollback) | command pane |
176:| `prefix + E` | **run any command** in the pane's cwd — fzf-pick from history or type it; the popup closes itself when the command exits ([details](#run-any-command)) | command **popup** |
300:- **Full server restart / reboot / crash.** `[session]` in the config exposes `resume_agents_on_restore = true` — resumes supported AI-agent panes back into their *native conversation sessions* after a server restart (requires the official `herdr integration install <agent>` hooks) — plus an option to save recent pane screen history across restarts. This covers the tmux-resurrect/continuum case natively, gated on those keys + integrations.
369:`prefix + G` proves the shape — a transient pane that runs something and vanishes when it exits — but its command is hardcoded. `prefix + E` is the generalisation: **fzf-pick a command from shell history (or just type a new one), it runs in the focused pane's cwd, and the popup closes itself on exit.** Helper: `~/.config/herdr/run-command.sh` = [`dot_config/herdr/executable_run-command.sh`](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles/blob/main/dot_config/herdr/executable_run-command.sh).
390:| **picker** | fzf over `$HISTFILE` (default `~/.zsh_history`), newest-first and de-duplicated. **Enter** runs the highlighted history entry; **`Alt+Enter` runs exactly what you typed**, even when history still matches it; typing something with no match at all and pressing Enter also runs it as a new command; `Esc` runs nothing. Falls back to a plain `read` prompt when fzf is absent |
394:> Two portability traps are handled inside the helper and are worth knowing if you edit it: `~/.zsh_history` is extended-history format (`: <ts>:<elapsed>;<cmd>`) **and contains non-UTF8 bytes**, so BSD `sed` aborts with `sed: RE error: illegal byte sequence` unless the parse runs under `LC_ALL=C`; and the newest-first reversal uses POSIX `awk` because `tail -r` is BSD-only while `tac` is GNU-only.
396:> **Why `Alt+Enter` had to exist.** Plain Enter cannot express *"run exactly what I typed"* while fzf still has a match — type `ls -la` with `ls -la /tmp` in history and Enter takes the history entry, which makes the picker feel like it can only replay old commands. `--expect=alt-enter` adds the escape hatch. Note that fzf's line layout is **not fixed**: with `--print-query --expect`, a no-match Enter prints only the query (one line), while an accepted match prints query / key / selection. The helper therefore reads the key from line 2 (empty or absent ⇒ plain Enter) and only trusts line 3 on exit code 0.
407:| `content` (scrollback) | `prefix+S` | *Copy pane: content (scrollback)* | the pane's full retained scrollback (`--source recent`) |
444:| Scope | **Visible screen by default** (matches tmux-fzf-url). `url-pick.sh <pane> --source recent` scans the full retained scrollback |
465:`path:line:col` suffixes (grep `-n` / stack traces / compiler output) are stripped before the existence test, so `pkg.py:42:5` validates as `pkg.py`. Scope is the visible screen by default (`--source recent` for scrollback); multi-select copies newline-joined; an empty result prints `no file paths found` and pauses ~1.5 s.
474:- **OSC133 copy-mode** (`cpout` / `cpblock`, prompt-jump, last-output yank) is tmux-specific. herdr's copy mode (`prefix+[`) is vi-style but has no OSC133 prompt-boundary awareness. `cpcmd` (zsh history, multiplexer-agnostic) still works.

```text
3:[ogulcancelik/herdr](https://github.com/ogulcancelik/herdr) is a Rust terminal multiplexer with **built-in coding-agent awareness** (it tracks per-pane agent state: idle / working / blocked / done). It sits in the same niche as tmux/zellij but is mouse-first and agent-native. Docs: <https://herdr.dev/docs/>.
5:This repo ships herdr as a **trial tool that coexists with tmux** — you run `herdr` *or* `tmux`, never nested. Nothing about the existing tmux / `sesh` / `tmuxp` / workmux setup changes; herdr is purely additive so you can evaluate it without losing your daily driver.
29:> **Not gated by `enableVimMode`.** That flag governs shell + tmux modal editing; herdr's copy mode (`prefix+[`) is vi-style natively regardless (`h/j/k/l`, `w/b/e`, `{`/`}`, `v`/Space to select, `y`/Enter to copy, `q`/Esc to leave), so there is nothing to gate.
33:## Model differences vs tmux
35:herdr's hierarchy is **Session → Workspace → Tab → Pane** — one level deeper than tmux (Session → Window → Pane). A "Workspace" is a project-level container; a "Tab" groups panes. The CLI (`herdr session|workspace|tab|pane|agent …`, most with `--json`) is the scripting surface that replaces `tmux switch-client` / `list-sessions` etc.
37:The important twist vs tmux: a single herdr **server hosts multiple named sessions**, each its own persistent tree with its own socket. That top **Session** level is closer to "multiple tmux servers / sockets" than to a tmux session — the tmux thing you'd call a session (`vibe/<repo>`) maps to a herdr **Workspace**, not a herdr Session.
78:Inside Herdr, **`prefix+Alt+F`** runs `herdr-grep --pick --visible`: type the grep pattern once, then use fzf to refine the already-filtered matches. Agent panes use Herdr's exact `agent focus`; ordinary split panes are reached through a validated shortest path of directional `pane neighbor` / `pane focus` calls, with final active workspace/tab plus `pane layout.focused_pane_id` verification. The picker refuses a different-session selection while already attached (detach first rather than nest). From a normal shell, `--pick --all-sessions` pre-focuses the selected target and then attaches its session, matching `hhere`'s focus-then-attach model. Preview line numbers refer to the earlier capture and may drift while the pane keeps printing.
86:herdr tracks cwd differently from tmux, which trips up two common expectations (all verified via `herdr pane list`):
92:- **A relative `--cwd` is resolved by the SERVER, and a miss falls back to `$HOME` silently.** `herdr workspace create --cwd ../foo` joins `../foo` to the directory `herdr server` was launched from — *not* to your shell's `$PWD` — and when that path doesn't exist herdr returns `{"result":{"type":"ok"}}` with the pane opened at `$HOME`. No error, no warning. **tmux is the opposite**: `new-session -c ../foo` is resolved client-side, which is why the `shere`/`scode`/`svibe` originals never needed a guard and their herdr ports did. Any user-supplied path must be absolutized in the calling shell before it reaches the CLI — `24_herdr.sh` does this in `_herdr_abs_dir`. See [`pitfalls/hhere-p-relative-path-opens-workspace-at-home.md`](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles/blob/main/pitfalls/hhere-p-relative-path-opens-workspace-at-home.md).
113:## Feasibility matrix (current tmux experience → herdr)
118:| Splits / zoom / new tab+workspace / pane nav | **Native** `[keys]` actions | Rebound to tmux muscle memory |
121:| Agent status 🤖/💬/✅ (workmux, 6 files) | **Native** agent-state rollups in sidebar | Skipped — native (workmux untouched for tmux). Panel ordered as an **attention queue**, not grouped by space: `ui.agent_panel_sort = "priority"` (herdr's default is `"spaces"`) |
122:| `sesh` fuzzy switch + `tmuxp` layouts | **Plugin** [herdr-plus](https://github.com/cloudmanic/herdr-plus) Projects + Quick Actions | Plugin + Projects templates |
125:| URL picker (`prefix+u`, tmux-fzf-url) | **Custom command pane + helper** | `prefix+u` → `url-pick.sh` (fzf → `x open`); `--source recent` scans scrollback |
126:| File-path picker (`prefix+p`; extrakto `prefix+Tab` on tmux) | **Custom command pane + helper** | `prefix+p` → `path-pick.sh` — two-tier (exists-under-cwd first) → `x copy` |
129:| OSC133 copy-mode (`cpout`/`cpblock`) | tmux-specific | **Gap** — `cpcmd` (zsh history) still works |
135:Prefix is `ctrl+b` (same as tmux). Built-in actions can only be *rebound* (herdr's action set is fixed); everything else is a `[[keys.command]]` custom command. Custom commands receive `$HERDR_SOCKET_PATH`, `$HERDR_ACTIVE_PANE_ID`, `$HERDR_ACTIVE_PANE_CWD` and run from the focused pane's cwd.
144:| `prefix + \|` / `prefix + %` · `prefix + minus` / `prefix + "` | split side-by-side / stacked (tmux muscle memory — both the intuitive key and the tmux default) | rebound (arrays) |
154:| `prefix + ,` | rename tab | rebound (tmux muscle memory) |
161:| `` prefix + u `` | **URL picker** — fzf-pick a URL from the pane and open it (`x open`); tmux-fzf-url analog. `--source recent` = full scrollback | command pane |
207:Four shell functions in [`dot_config/shell/24_herdr.sh`](../shells/aliases.md#session-management) are the herdr counterparts of the tmux `svibe` / `scode` / `shere` / `sroot` helpers. The two **heavyweight** ones (`hvibe` / `hcode`) spin up a whole coding workspace in one motion; the two **lightweight** ones (`hhere` / `hroot`) just open a plain workspace at a directory and attach — no git repo, no agent layout. They shell out to the native `herdr workspace|tab|pane` CLI and **reuse the pure logic verbatim** (specstory wrapping, `--on-exit shell|kill|restart`, git-root resolution, agent-CLI detection) from `22_sesh.sh`; only the layout calls differ. Need the `herdr` server running + `jq`.
217:- **The plain-open pair (`hhere` / `hroot`)** fills the gap where every other herdr entry point forces a git repo + a full agent layout. With tmux, `tmux new-session` lands you in `$PWD` directly; herdr adds a Workspace layer, so without these you'd launch herdr, create a space (which opens at `$HOME` per `new_cwd`), then `cd` by hand. `hhere` does the one-shot: `herdr workspace create --cwd "$PWD"` → focus → attach if outside. No git requirement; the optional command runs **raw** (no specstory/on-exit wrapping — that stays with `hcode`/`hvibe`). `hhere -h` / `hroot -h` for flags. **Label caveat**: herdr auto-relabels a workspace to its root pane's *live* cwd basename after a `cd` in tab 1 (see the **cwd & workspace-naming model** section above), so the idempotent-focus is best-effort — a drifted label makes a re-run open a fresh workspace. **`-p DIR` is absolutized in your shell** (via `_herdr_abs_dir`, shared with `hcode`/`hvibe`) before it reaches herdr, so relative paths like `hhere -p ../sibling` work and a typo'd DIR is a hard error instead of a silent workspace at `$HOME` — see the `--cwd` bullet in the cwd model section for why that guard exists.
219:- **Attach-aware (like svibe's `$TMUX` branch)**: run from **inside** herdr → the workspace/tab focus calls switch the live client (no new client). Run from a **plain terminal outside** herdr → the helper brings up a client attached to the session so the new workspace is actually visible (herdr's `workspace focus` only moves an *already-attached* client, so without this the pack was built invisibly). `--no-attach` builds detached either way. Detection is the ambient `HERDR_ENV`.
225:The tmux `svibe` / `scode` remain the tmux-side equivalents (see [sesh](sesh.md)); the two families coexist — `hvibe`/`hcode` only touch herdr, `svibe`/`scode` only touch tmux.
227:## herdr-plus plugin (sesh + tmuxp + menu analog)
229:[herdr-plus](https://github.com/cloudmanic/herdr-plus) adds **Projects** (declarative multi-tab/multi-pane workspace templates with a fuzzy picker — the `tmuxp`/`tmuxinator` analog) and **Quick Actions** (a fuzzy command launcher — the popup-menu analog).
239:Project templates are chezmoi-managed under `dot_config/herdr/plugins/config/cloudmanic.herdr-plus/projects/` → the same path under `~/.config/`. The shipped `chezmoi.toml` mirrors this repo's tmuxinator `chezmoi` session (editor/git/shell tabs). Bind `prefix+O` → Projects and `prefix+y` → Quick Actions (already in the config).
247:Most `tv` channels (`tools`, `fleet-hosts`, `mlflow`, `kill-process`, `ssh-config`) have **non-tmux-coupled actions**, so they run unchanged in a herdr command pane — just bind a key to `tv <channel>`. Only the channels whose actions call `tmux …` need herdr-aware variants. Three ship here:
249:- `herdr-sesh` (`dot_config/television/cable/herdr-sesh.toml`) — lists herdr sessions/workspaces + zoxide dirs; Enter dispatches `herdr session attach` / `herdr workspace focus` / `herdr workspace create --cwd` instead of `sesh connect` / `tmux switch-client`. `Ctrl+D` closes the selected workspace; **`Alt+Y` copies its directory** (works on workspace *and* zoxide-dir rows — see [`dir` vs `cwd`](#space-dir)). The preview shows that derived dir above the raw `workspace get` JSON, so you can see what `Alt+Y` will hand you.
253:The original tmux-bound `sesh` / `agent-panes` channels are left intact for coexistence.
```

 `./docs/tools/clipboard.md`

```text
1	# Clipboard & OSC 52
2	
3	This doc explains how clipboard sync is wired across this dotfiles setup, with a focus on **OSC 52** — the escape sequence that lets a remote SSH session put text on your **local** machine's clipboard.
4	
5	## TL;DR
6	
7	| You are… | Yank in Neovim goes to… | Capture pane (`prefix+y/Y/C-y`) goes to… |
8	|----------|--------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
9	| Local (macOS or Linux desktop) | system clipboard (default provider: `pbcopy` / `wl-copy` / `xclip`) | same, via `tmux load-buffer -w -` which emits OSC 52 *and* sets tmux's paste buffer |
10	| SSH (remote box, with or without tmux) | **local** machine's clipboard (via OSC 52) | **local** machine's clipboard (via tmux → OSC 52) |
11	
12	No extra tools, no X forwarding, no socat listener needed. The only hard requirement is a terminal emulator on your **local** machine that supports OSC 52 (Ghostty, Alacritty, iTerm2, Kitty, WezTerm — all do).
13	
14	## What is OSC 52?
15	
16	`OSC 52` is an ANSI escape sequence:
17	
18	```
19	ESC ] 52 ; c ; <base64-of-data> BEL
20	```
21	
22	Any program that can write to a terminal can emit this sequence; the terminal emulator on the other end decodes the base64 and writes it to the system clipboard. The crucial property: **escape sequences travel up the TTY back to the client terminal**, so this works transparently over SSH, mosh, and nested `tmux ssh` chains — no display server, no socket forwarding.
23	
24	Tradeoffs:
25	
26	- **Write** is ubiquitous. Most modern terminals allow it by default or with a simple opt-in.
27	- **Read** (paste from local clipboard back into remote apps) is much less supported — many terminals refuse for obvious security reasons (a malicious server could exfiltrate your clipboard). Ghostty prompts; Alacritty flat-out ignores it.
28	- A terminal multiplexer (tmux, screen, zellij) sits between the inner app and the outer terminal. It must be configured to either **emit** OSC 52 to its host terminal or **pass through** OSC 52 from inner apps.
29	- **Text only** — OSC 52 carries base64 *text*; it cannot move an **image** (or file object) from your local clipboard into a remote app, and it flows remote→local, the wrong direction for feeding a screenshot to a remote agent. Getting a local screenshot into a remote coding agent (Claude Code / Neovim) is a separate problem — see [`remote-image-paste.md`](./remote-image-paste.md).
30	
31	Reference: [tmux Clipboard wiki](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/wiki/Clipboard), [XTerm control sequences (OSC)](https://www.invisible-island.net/xterm/ctlseqs/ctlseqs.html).
32	
33	## How this repo wires it up
34	
35	Four layers cooperate. Removing any one silently breaks remote-clipboard sync.
36	
37	### 1. Terminal emulator (outer, on your local machine)
38	
39	Must accept OSC 52 writes from whatever is running inside it.
40	
41	**Ghostty / cmux** — [`dot_config/ghostty/config`](../../dot_config/ghostty/config):
42	
43	```conf
44	clipboard-write = allow   # let inner apps set the system clipboard
45	clipboard-read  = ask     # prompt before reads (safer default)
46	```
47	
48	Both match current Ghostty defaults but are pinned explicitly so policy drifts from upstream don't silently break (or weaken) this chain.
49	
50	**Alacritty** — native support, no config needed. Paste from OSC 52 not supported.
51	
52	**iTerm2 / Kitty / WezTerm** — native support. iTerm2 requires `Preferences → General → Selection → Applications in terminal may access clipboard` for reads.
53	
54	### 2. Multiplexer — tmux
55	
56	[`dot_config/tmux/common.conf`](../../dot_config/tmux/common.conf):
57	
58	```tmux
59	set -g set-clipboard on
60	
61	set -as terminal-features ",xterm*:clipboard"
62	set -as terminal-features ",ghostty*:clipboard"
63	set -as terminal-features ",alacritty*:clipboard"
64	
65	set -g allow-passthrough on
66	```
67	
68	- **`set-clipboard on`** — tmux both re-emits OSC 52 to the outer terminal when its own copy-mode yanks, and passes OSC 52 from inner apps (Neovim, less, etc.) through. `external` would only pass through; `on` is a strict superset and simpler.
69	- **`terminal-features …:clipboard`** — tells tmux the outer terminal supports OSC 52 without needing a terminfo `Ms` capability. Many distros ship a `tmux-256color` entry that lacks `Ms`, so declaring the feature directly avoids surprises when `chezmoi apply` is run on a fresh box.
70	- **`allow-passthrough on`** — lets terminal-image protocols (sixel, kitty graphics) work; also covers OSC passthrough for nested multiplexers.
71	
72	**Capture-pane helpers** — [`dot_config/tmux/keybindings.conf`](../../dot_config/tmux/keybindings.conf) — use the tmux-native idiom rather than shelling out:
73	
74	```tmux
75	bind y   run-shell "tmux capture-pane -p   | tmux load-buffer -w -"
76	bind Y   run-shell "tmux capture-pane -pS - | tmux load-buffer -w -"
77	bind C-y run-shell "tmux capture-pane -pS - | fzf-tmux … | tmux load-buffer -w -"
78	```
79	
80	`load-buffer -w -` reads stdin into tmux's paste buffer *and* (because of `-w`) forwards to the system clipboard via OSC 52. Previously these bindings used a `pbcopy | xclip | xsel` fallback chain that only worked locally — over SSH they copied to the **remote** machine's clipboard, which is useless. The tmux-native form works identically in both places.
81	
82	`set-buffer -w …` offers the same `-w` flag but takes data as an argument, which introduces shell-quoting landmines on multi-line pane content; `load-buffer -w -` reads stdin and sidesteps that.
83	
84	### 3. Editor — Neovim
85	
86	[`dot_config/nvim/lua/config/options.lua`](../../dot_config/nvim/lua/config/options.lua):
87	
88	```lua
89	vim.opt.clipboard = "unnamedplus"
90	
91	if vim.env.SSH_CONNECTION or vim.env.SSH_TTY then
92	  local osc52 = require("vim.ui.clipboard.osc52")
93	  vim.g.clipboard = {
94	    name = "OSC 52",
95	    copy  = { ["+"] = osc52.copy("+"),  ["*"] = osc52.copy("*")  },
96	    paste = { ["+"] = osc52.paste("+"), ["*"] = osc52.paste("*") },
97	  }
98	end
99	```
100	
101	- Locally, LazyVim's default provider is used (`pbcopy`/`xclip`/`wl-copy` — with working paste).
102	- Over SSH, Neovim's built-in `vim.ui.clipboard.osc52` (shipping since Neovim 0.10) emits OSC 52 directly, bypassing any `pbcopy` binary on the remote host.
103	- The check is `SSH_CONNECTION or SSH_TTY` — either is set by `sshd` for an interactive session.
104	
105	Why conditional rather than always-on OSC 52? OSC 52 paste is unreliable (see the terminal table above). Keeping the local provider for local sessions preserves Neovim's paste behaviour; the override only activates when `pbcopy` on the remote is clearly the wrong answer.
106	
107	### 4. Shell CLI — `x` (cross-platform clipboard wrapper)
108	
109	[`dot_dotfiles/bin/executable_x`](../../dot_dotfiles/bin/executable_x) (deployed to `~/.dotfiles/bin/x`) is a Bash wrapper with three subcommands:
110	
111	```bash
112	printf "hello" | x copy        # copy stdin to clipboard
113	x copy path/to/file            # copy file contents
114	x copy-file path/to/file       # copy file object (paste into Finder / Files)
115	x paste                        # print clipboard to stdout
116	x open https://example.com     # open URL/file in default app
117	```
118	
119	Its copy backend tries, in order: `clip.exe` (WSL) → `pbcopy` (macOS) → `wl-copy` (Wayland) → `xclip` → `xsel` → **OSC 52 fallback** writing directly to `/dev/tty`. This means `x copy` Just Works on macOS, Linux desktop, Linux SSH server, WSL, and anything else that can reach a terminal — you never have to think about which backend is available.
120	
121	`x copy-file PATH...` is intentionally separate from `x copy PATH`: it places file objects on the desktop clipboard so a file manager can paste/copy the selected files, instead of pasting the files' text contents. It uses macOS `osascript` on Finder-compatible desktops and Linux `x-special/gnome-copied-files` MIME data via `wl-copy` / `xclip` for common GTK file managers. This is local-desktop only; OSC 52 cannot carry file objects over SSH. For remote hosts, copy contents with `x copy FILE` or copy a path with `realpath FILE | x copy`.
122	
123	The OSC 52 fallback in `x` is also wrapped for tmux:
124	
125	```bash
126	if [[ -n "${TMUX:-}" ]]; then
127	  printf '\033Ptmux;\033\033]52;c;%s\033\033\\\033\\' "$data" > /dev/tty
128	else
129	  printf '\033]52;c;%s\033\\' "$data" > /dev/tty
130	fi
131	```
132	
133	The `DCS tmux; ... ST` wrapper is tmux's passthrough escape — it tells tmux "hand this sequence to the outer terminal as-is", needed because tmux otherwise intercepts OSC 52.
134	
135	## Verifying the chain works
136	
137	On the remote box where Neovim yank is misbehaving, run:
138	
139	```bash
140	# tmux: does it believe the terminal can accept OSC 52?
141	tmux info | grep -Ei 'clipboard|Ms:'
142	# expect: clipboard: true  and an Ms entry that is NOT [missing]
143	
144	# shell: can x copy reach the clipboard?
145	printf "hello from %s" "$(hostname)" | x copy
146	# then Cmd+V / Ctrl+V into a local app → should paste "hello from <remote-host>"
147	
148	# Neovim: which provider is active?
149	nvim -c ':checkhealth provider.clipboard' -c ':only'
150	# expect: OSC 52 under SSH, native under local
151	```
152	
153	If `tmux info` shows `clipboard: false` after editing `common.conf`, remember a running tmux server **keeps its old capability table** — `tmux kill-server` (losing sessions; `tmux-resurrect` can restore them) and re-attach.
154	
155	## Common failure modes
156	
157	| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
158	|---------|-------------|-----|
159	| Yank works outside tmux but vanishes inside tmux (remote) | `set-clipboard off` or server running pre-edit binary | `tmux show -g set-clipboard`; `tmux kill-server` |
160	| `tmux info` shows `Ms: [missing]` | tmux's TERM entry lacks `Ms` *and* no `terminal-features …:clipboard` declared | already handled by [`common.conf`](../../dot_config/tmux/common.conf); on an unusual outer `$TERM`, add another `set -as terminal-features` line |
161	| Ghostty asks about clipboard every yank | `clipboard-read = ask`; Ghostty interprets some writes as reads when apps immediately re-fetch | switch to `clipboard-read = allow` if you trust everything inside your sessions |
162	| Neovim yank works, but `"*p` does nothing over SSH | paste over OSC 52 not supported by outer terminal | expected — use mouse middle-click or re-type; don't fight it |
163	| `prefix+y` still copies to remote clipboard | shim binary `tmux` resolves to an old pre-`load-buffer -w` version | `tmux -V` must be ≥ 3.3 for `load-buffer -w`; this repo enforces ≥ 3.3 via ansible `devtools` role |
164	| Nested tmux (`tmux inside ssh inside tmux`) | inner tmux eats OSC 52 | inner tmux needs `set -g allow-passthrough on`; already on in this config. Double-nested cases may require `Ptmux;…` wrapping |
165	
166	## Design notes / non-defaults
167	
168	- **tmux `set-clipboard`** is `on`, not `external`. `external` disables tmux's own OSC 52 emission from copy-mode; `on` is a superset and keeps `prefix+[` → `y` working.
169	- **Neovim OSC 52 provider** is gated on `SSH_CONNECTION`/`SSH_TTY` rather than always-on, specifically so local paste (`"+p`) continues to work. If you primarily work over SSH and don't mind the paste tradeoff, the `if …` block can be removed.
170	- **`x` CLI ordering** prefers local backends (`pbcopy`, `wl-copy`, etc.) over OSC 52. This is intentional: when `pbcopy` is available, it's faster, doesn't touch the TTY, and works for very large payloads (OSC 52 payloads are size-limited by the terminal — iTerm2 caps at 1 MB, many others at 64-256 KB).
171	
172	## Clipboard history (`cb` / `cbl` / `cbe`)
173	
174	OSC 52 covers **sync** — getting yanked text from a remote box to your local clipboard. Clipboard *history* — recalling something you copied an hour ago — is a separate concern with a separate backend, wrapped behind a unified shell API by [`dot_config/shell/56_clipboard_history.sh`](../../dot_config/shell/56_clipboard_history.sh).
175	
176	### Hybrid backend
177	
178	| OS | Backend | Install | CLI surface |
179	|----|---------|---------|------------|
180	| macOS | **Maccy** | `brew install --cask maccy` (signed, healthy on brew, auto-updating, macOS 14+) | None shipped — helper queries Maccy's plaintext SQLite directly |
181	| Ubuntu desktop | **CopyQ** | `sudo apt install copyq` (stock 22.04 / 24.04 repos; ansible role: [`gui_apps_linux`](../../dot_ansible/roles/gui_apps_linux/tasks/main.yml)) | `copyq read / select / eval / size / copy` |
182	| Ubuntu server | — | none | helper prints install hint and returns 1 |
183	
184	Why hybrid rather than CopyQ everywhere: the **CopyQ Homebrew cask** is deprecated (disabled 2026-09-01) because `CopyQ.app` is not signed for macOS Gatekeeper. Only the cask is affected — the upstream project is fine, and the Linux package is unaffected (see [hluk/CopyQ#3498](https://github.com/hluk/CopyQ/issues/3498)). Maccy is the most maintained signed-and-on-brew clipboard manager for macOS; the trade-off is no shipped CLI, so we query the plaintext SQLite at `~/Library/Application Support/Maccy/Storage.sqlite` (cask install) or `~/Library/Containers/org.p0deje.Maccy/.../Storage.sqlite` (Mac App Store sandboxed).
185	
186	### API
187	
188	| Command | Behaviour |
189	|---------|-----------|
190	| `cbl [N]` | List recent `N` clipboard items (default 20), tab-separated `<idx>\t<first-line-preview>`. Filters to UTF-8 plain text only. |
191	| `cb` | Pipe `cbl 100` to fzf → selected item is moved to the top of the stack and copied to the system clipboard. CopyQ uses `copyq select`; Maccy uses `pbcopy` (Maccy then re-records, adding a duplicate at index 0 — known quirk, not a bug). |
192	| `cbe` | Same fzf flow as `cb`, but reads the item into a tempfile, opens `$EDITOR`, then writes the edited contents back to the clipboard. |
193	
194	The first column of `cbl`'s output is:
195	- For CopyQ: the position index (`0` = top of stack)
196	- For Maccy: the SQLite `Z_PK` primary key
197	
198	This is intentional — each backend can address its own items round-trip without translation.
199	
200	### Manual backend override
201	
202	Set `CLIP_BACKEND=copyq` or `CLIP_BACKEND=maccy` to skip autodetect (useful if both are installed on the same mac and you want the more-reliable CopyQ CLI):
203	
204	```sh
205	CLIP_BACKEND=copyq cb     # one-off
206	export CLIP_BACKEND=copyq  # session
207	```
208	
209	Unknown values print a hint and return 1.
210	
211	### Coexistence with Raycast
212	
213	On macOS the new helper does **not** disable Raycast's clipboard module — both will record every `⌘C` independently. Two separate histories, no functional conflict, slight storage duplication. To disable: Raycast → Extensions → Clipboard History → toggle off.
214	
215	### Threat model — secrets in plaintext
216	
217	Both Maccy and CopyQ store unencrypted SQLite. Anything you copy from a terminal / browser / text editor as plain text (e.g. `cat .env`, an API key pasted from Slack) lands in the DB readable by your own shell.
218	
219	What is NOT recorded:
220	- macOS pasteboard items marked `org.nspasteboard.ConcealedType` / `TransientType` / `AutoGeneratedType`. 1Password, Bitwarden, KeePassXC, Keychain Access all set these — secrets pasted via those tools never enter the history.
221	- Anything copied while Maccy's "Ignore Events" toggle (`⌥`-click menu icon) or CopyQ's "Disable Clipboard Storing" is active.
222	
223	For ad-hoc secret pastes, toggle "Ignore" before pasting and toggle off after.
224	
225	### DB paths (for backup / inspection)
226	
227	- Maccy (cask): `~/Library/Application Support/Maccy/Storage.sqlite` (+ `-wal`, `-shm`)
228	- Maccy (Mac App Store): `~/Library/Containers/org.p0deje.Maccy/Data/Library/Application Support/Maccy/Storage.sqlite`
229	- CopyQ: `~/.config/copyq/` on Linux, `~/Library/Application Support/copyq/` on macOS
230	
231	The Maccy schema is documented in the [helper file's header comment](../../dot_config/shell/56_clipboard_history.sh) — verified against `p0deje/Maccy@master` source files (`HistoryItem.swift` + `HistoryItemContent.swift`).
232	
233	## Related docs
234	
235	- [Remote image paste (SSH)](./remote-image-paste.md) — the image-shaped sequel: getting a local screenshot into a remote coding agent (OSC 52 can't)
236	- [tmux](./tmux/README.md) — "OSC 52 Clipboard (SSH-friendly yank)" section
237	- [Ghostty](./ghostty.md) — terminal-side notes
238	- [`dot_dotfiles/bin/executable_x`](../../dot_dotfiles/bin/executable_x) — the `x` wrapper source
239	- [`dot_config/shell/56_clipboard_history.sh`](../../dot_config/shell/56_clipboard_history.sh) — clipboard-history backend dispatch
240	
241	## External references
242	
243	- [tmux Clipboard wiki](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/wiki/Clipboard)
244	- [Neovim `:help clipboard-osc52`](https://neovim.io/doc/user/provider.html#clipboard-osc52)
245	- [XTerm OSC 52 spec](https://www.invisible-island.net/xterm/ctlseqs/ctlseqs.html#h3-Operating-System-Commands)
246
```

## Root Cause Investigation: `content --source recent` OSC 52 clipboard failure

### 1. Which backend fires during a bare SSH session

Confirmed by reading `dot_dotfiles/bin/executable_x` in full (`copy_backend()`, lines 141-189):

```
141  copy_backend() {
142      if is_wsl && command -v clip.exe ...        # WSL only
150      if command -v pbcopy ...                     # macOS only
158      if [[ -n "${WAYLAND_DISPLAY:-}" ]] && wl-copy  # needs WAYLAND_DISPLAY
166      if [[ -n "${DISPLAY:-}" ]] && xclip            # needs DISPLAY
174      if [[ -n "${DISPLAY:-}" ]] && xsel             # needs DISPLAY
182      # Final fallback: OSC 52 (works over SSH, no display needed).
183      if osc52_copy; then
184          return 0
```

Over a bare SSH session (no `DISPLAY`/`WAYLAND_DISPLAY`, not macOS/WSL), every guarded branch is skipped and `osc52_copy()` (lines 61-76) is the backend that actually fires — exactly as the bug report assumed.

### 2. `osc52_copy()` has no size limit or chunking

```
61  osc52_copy() {
62      [[ -w /dev/tty ]] || return 1
63      command -v base64 >/dev/null 2>&1 || return 1
64
65      local data
66      data="$(base64 | tr -d '\n')"
67      [[ -n "$data" ]] || return 0
68
69      if [[ -n "${TMUX:-}" ]]; then
70          printf '\033Ptmux;\033\033]52;c;%s\033\033\\\033\\' "$data" > /dev/tty
71      else
72          printf '\033]52;c;%s\033\\' "$data" > /dev/tty
73      fi
74  }
```

No length check, no truncation warning, no chunked multi-sequence write — the entire base64 payload (whole pane scrollback, possibly hundreds of KB) is shoved into a single `printf ... > /dev/tty` call, unconditionally.

### 3. The repo's own docs already state the size-limit fact — and it directly explains the symptom

`docs/tools/clipboard.md:170` (Design notes section):

> **`x` CLI ordering** prefers local backends (`pbcopy`, `wl-copy`, etc.) over OSC 52. This is intentional: when `pbcopy` is available, it's faster, doesn't touch the TTY, and works for very large payloads (**OSC 52 payloads are size-limited by the terminal — iTerm2 caps at 1 MB, many others at 64-256 KB**).

This is the smoking gun: the repo already knows and documents that OSC 52 has a hard, terminal-imposed payload ceiling (as low as 64 KB in many terminals), yet nothing in `osc52_copy()` or `pane-copy.sh` checks payload size before sending, or falls back/warns when it's exceeded. A full pane scrollback (`herdr pane read --source recent`) easily produces tens to hundreds of KB of text — base64 inflates that ~1.33x — so it plausibly blows past the terminal's cap while `process-info`/`coord`/`cwd`/`dir` (a handful of lines) stay comfortably under any limit. That precisely matches the reported pattern: small payloads succeed, only the scrollback copy silently fails.

Notably, `docs/tools/clipboard.md`'s "Common failure modes" table (lines 155-164) does **not** list this large-payload/silent-drop case — so it's a real, previously undocumented gap, not a known/already-mitigated issue.

### 4. herdr is not run nested inside tmux (per this repo's design) — tmux's `history-limit` is irrelevant here

`docs/tools/herdr.md:5`:

> This repo ships herdr as a **trial tool that coexists with tmux** — you run `herdr` *or* `tmux`, never nested.

Since herdr and tmux are not nested by design, `$TMUX` is unset in a plain SSH+herdr session, so `osc52_copy()` takes the *non*-tmux branch (`executable_x:72`, plain `ESC ] 52 ; c ; ... ST`) — bypassing tmux's `set -g history-limit 50000` (`dot_config/tmux/common.conf.tmpl:80`) and its `set-clipboard on` OSC 52 relay entirely. Those tmux settings only matter for tmux's own copy-mode/`load-buffer -w` path (`docs/tools/tmux/README.md:89-95`, `docs/tools/clipboard.md:54-83`), which is a completely separate code path from herdr's `pane-copy.sh` → `x copy`. So the raw OSC 52 sequence goes straight from the SSH session's shell to whatever local terminal emulator the user's SSH client is running in, and that terminal's own (undocumented-per-terminal, but known to be small — 64 KB-1 MB per `docs/tools/clipboard.md:170`) cap is the actual bottleneck.

I found **no herdr-side scrollback/history size cap** configured in `.chezmoitemplates/herdr/config.toml` — the file's header (line 11) explicitly notes `[session]` (herdr's own runtime scrollback-retention settings) is left as whatever herdr writes/preserves at runtime, not overridden by this repo's config overlay. So this isn't a herdr-truncates-`recent`-itself issue; the size that ultimately hits the terminal is whatever herdr's live retained scrollback for that pane happened to be.

### 5. Does the "copied" success message get printed regardless of actual delivery? Yes.

`dot_config/herdr/executable_pane-copy.sh:140-143`:

```
140  body=$(herdr pane read "$pane" --source "$source" --format text 2>/dev/null) \
141      || { echo "pane-copy: failed to read content of $pane" >&2; exit 1; }
142  copy "$body"
143  echo "copied $source content for $pane"
```

`copy()` is defined at line 89: `copy() { printf '%s' "$1" | "$X_BIN" copy; }`.

The script runs under `set -eu` (line 41, no `pipefail`), so `copy "$body"`'s exit status is `x copy`'s exit status. But `osc52_copy()`'s `printf ... > /dev/tty` (`executable_x:71-73`) is a plain write to a character device — the `write(2)` syscall succeeds as soon as the kernel/pty accepts the bytes, completely independent of whether the (possibly remote, multi-hop-SSH) terminal emulator on the other end actually parses, accepts, or silently drops/truncates an oversized OSC 52 escape sequence. There is no ack/handshake in the OSC 52 protocol. So `osc52_copy` returns 0 → `copy_backend` returns 0 → `x copy` exits 0 → `copy "$body"` returns 0 → line 143's `echo "copied $source content for $pane"` fires unconditionally, even when the terminal silently discarded the escape sequence because it exceeded the size cap.

**This confirms the tool is structurally incapable of detecting or reporting this failure mode** — success is reported based purely on the local write to `/dev/tty` succeeding, not on any terminal-side acknowledgment (which OSC 52 as a protocol doesn't provide anyway).

### Summary — root cause ranking

1. **Primary (best-supported) hypothesis**: `osc52_copy()` in `dot_dotfiles/bin/executable_x:61-76` has no payload-size check or chunking. Full pane scrollback (`content --source recent`) can exceed the local terminal's OSC 52 size cap (documented in this same repo, `docs/tools/clipboard.md:170`, as low as 64-256 KB for many terminals, 1 MB for iTerm2), while `process`/`coord`/`cwd`/`dir` payloads are tiny and always stay under any such limit — matching the reported pattern exactly.
2. **Compounding factor**: OSC 52 has no delivery acknowledgment, and a `printf ... > /dev/tty` write succeeds at the OS level regardless of terminal-side acceptance, so `x copy` (and therefore `pane-copy.sh`'s "copied … content" message at line 143) reports success unconditionally — the failure is silent by design of the escape-sequence mechanism, not a logic bug in error handling that could be trivially fixed by checking exit codes.
3. **Ruled out / not the cause**: tmux's `history-limit 50000` (`dot_config/tmux/common.conf.tmpl:80`) and `set-clipboard on` — these only govern tmux's own copy-mode → OSC 52 relay path, which is not in play since herdr and tmux are designed to run un-nested (`docs/tools/herdr.md:5`), so `$TMUX` is unset and `osc52_copy()`'s plain (non-DCS-wrapped) branch is used, going straight from the SSH shell to the user's local terminal.
4. **Ruled out**: herdr's own scrollback retention (`--source recent`) — no explicit size/line cap is configured by this repo's `.chezmoitemplates/herdr/config.toml` overlay; that setting is left to herdr's own runtime `[session]` config, unmanaged here, so there's no evidence the failure originates from herdr trimming/limiting `recent` content before it ever reaches `x copy`.

So the raw OSC 52 sequence goes straight from the SSH session's shell to whatever local terminal emulator the user's SSH client is running in, and that terminal's own (undocumented-per-terminal, but known to be small — 64 KB-1 MB per `docs/tools/clipboard.md:170`) cap is the actual bottleneck.

I found **no herdr-side scrollback/history size cap** configured in `.chezmoitemplates/herdr/config.toml` — the file's header (line 11) explicitly notes `[session]` (herdr's own runtime scrollback-retention settings) is left as whatever herdr writes/preserves at runtime, not overridden by this repo's config overlay. So this isn't a herdr-truncates-`recent`-itself issue; the size that ultimately hits the terminal is whatever herdr's live retained scrollback for that pane happened to be.

### 5. Does the "copied" success message get printed regardless of actual delivery? Yes.

`dot_config/herdr/executable_pane-copy.sh:140-143`:

```
140  body=$(herdr pane read "$pane" --source "$source" --format text 2&gt;/dev/null) \
141      || { echo "pane-copy: failed to read content of $pane" &gt;&amp;2; exit 1; }
142  copy "$body"
143  echo "copied $source content for $pane"
```

`copy()` is defined at line 89: `copy() { printf '%s' "$1" | "$X_BIN" copy; }`.

The script runs under `set -eu` (line 41, no `pipefail`), so `copy "$body"`'s exit status is `x copy`'s exit status. But `osc52_copy()`'s `printf ... &gt; /dev/tty` (`executable_x:71-73`) is a plain write to a character device — the `write(2)` syscall succeeds as soon as the kernel/pty accepts the bytes, completely independent of whether the (possibly remote, multi-hop-SSH) terminal emulator on the other end actually parses, accepts, or silently drops/truncates an oversized OSC 52 escape sequence. There is no ack/handshake in the OSC 52 protocol. So `osc52_copy` returns 0 → `copy_backend` returns 0 → `x copy` exits 0 → `copy "$body"` returns 0 → line 143's `echo "copied $source content for $pane"` fires unconditionally, even when the terminal silently discarded the escape sequence because it exceeded the size cap.

**This confirms the tool is structurally incapable of detecting or reporting this failure mode** — success is reported based purely on the local write to `/dev/tty` succeeding, not on any terminal-side acknowledgment (which OSC 52 as a protocol doesn't provide anyway).

### Summary — root cause ranking

1. **Primary (best-supported) hypothesis**: `osc52_copy()` in `dot_dotfiles/bin/executable_x:61-76` has no payload-size check or chunking. Full pane scrollback (`content --source recent`) can exceed the local terminal's OSC 52 size cap (documented in this same repo, `docs/tools/clipboard.md:170`, as low as 64-256 KB for many terminals, 1 MB for iTerm2), while `process`/`coord`/`cwd`/`dir` payloads are tiny and always stay under any such limit — matching the reported pattern exactly.
2. **Compounding factor**: OSC 52 has no delivery acknowledgment, and a `printf ... &gt; /dev/tty` write succeeds at the OS level regardless of terminal-side acceptance, so `x copy` (and therefore `pane-copy.sh`'s "copied … content" message at line 143) reports success unconditionally — the failure is silent by design of the escape-sequence mechanism, not a logic bug in error handling that could be trivially fixed by checking exit codes.
3. **Ruled out / not the cause**: tmux's `history-limit 50000` (`dot_config/tmux/common.conf.tmpl:80`) and `set-clipboard on` — these only govern tmux's own copy-mode → OSC 52 relay path, which is not in play since herdr and tmux are designed to run un-nested (`docs/tools/herdr.md:5`), so `$TMUX` is unset and `osc52_copy()`'s plain (non-DCS-wrapped) branch is used, going straight from the SSH shell to the user's local terminal.
4. **Ruled out**: herdr's own scrollback retention (`--source recent`) — no explicit size/line cap is configured by this repo's `.chezmoitemplates/herdr/config.toml` overlay; that setting is left to herdr's own runtime `[session]` config, unmanaged here, so there's no evidence the failure originates from herdr trimming/limiting `recent` content before it ever reaches `x copy`.</result>

152	
153	If `tmux info` shows `clipboard: false` after editing `common.conf`, remember a running tmux server **keeps its old capability table** — `tmux kill-server` (losing sessions; `tmux-resurrect` can restore them) and re-attach.
154	
155	## Common failure modes
156	
157	| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
158	|---------|-------------|-----|
159	| Yank works outside tmux but vanishes inside tmux (remote) | `set-clipboard off` or server running pre-edit binary | `tmux show -g set-clipboard`; `tmux kill-server` |
160	| `tmux info` shows `Ms: [missing]` | tmux's TERM entry lacks `Ms` *and* no `terminal-features …:clipboard` declared | already handled by [`common.conf`](../../dot_config/tmux/common.conf); on an unusual outer `$TERM`, add another `set -as terminal-features` line |
161	| Ghostty asks about clipboard every yank | `clipboard-read = ask`; Ghostty interprets some writes as reads when apps immediately re-fetch | switch to `clipboard-read = allow` if you trust everything inside your sessions |
162	| Neovim yank works, but `"*p` does nothing over SSH | paste over OSC 52 not supported by outer terminal | expected — use mouse middle-click or re-type; don't fight it |
163	| `prefix+y` still copies to remote clipboard | shim binary `tmux` resolves to an old pre-`load-buffer -w` version | `tmux -V` must be ≥ 3.3 for `load-buffer -w`; this repo enforces ≥ 3.3 via ansible `devtools` role |
164	| Nested tmux (`tmux inside ssh inside tmux`) | inner tmux eats OSC 52 | inner tmux needs `set -g allow-passthrough on`; already on in this config. Double-nested cases may require `Ptmux;…` wrapping |
165	
166	## Design notes / non-defaults
167	
168	- **tmux `set-clipboard`** is `on`, not `external`. `external` disables tmux's own OSC 52 emission from copy-mode; `on` is a superset and keeps `prefix+[` → `y` working.
169	- **Neovim OSC 52 provider** is gated on `SSH_CONNECTION`/`SSH_TTY` rather than always-on, specifically so local paste (`"+p`) continues to work. If you primarily work over SSH and don't mind the paste tradeoff, the `if …` block can be removed.
170	- **`x` CLI ordering** prefers local backends (`pbcopy`, `wl-copy`, etc.) over OSC 52. This is intentional: when `pbcopy` is available, it's faster, doesn't touch the TTY, and works for very large payloads (OSC 52 payloads are size-limited by the terminal — iTerm2 caps at 1 MB, many others at 64-256 KB).
171	
172	## Clipboard history (`cb` / `cbl` / `cbe`)
173	
174	OSC 52 covers **sync** — getting yanked text from a remote box to your local clipboard. Clipboard *history* — recalling something you copied an hour ago — is a separate concern with a separate backend, wrapped behind a unified shell API by [`dot_config/shell/56_clipboard_history.sh`](../../dot_config/shell/56_clipboard_history.sh).
175	
176	### Hybrid backend
177	
178	| OS | Backend | Install | CLI surface |
179	|----|---------|---------|------------|
180	| macOS | **Maccy** | `brew install --cask maccy` (signed, healthy on brew, auto-updating, macOS 14+) | None shipped — helper queries Maccy's plaintext SQLite directly |
181	| Ubuntu desktop | **CopyQ** | `sudo apt install copyq` (stock 22.04 / 24.04 repos; ansible role: [`gui_apps_linux`](../../dot_ansible/roles/gui_apps_linux/tasks/main.yml)) | `copyq read / select / eval / size / copy` |
182	| Ubuntu server | — | none | helper prints install hint and returns 1 |
183	
184	Why hybrid rather than CopyQ everywhere: the **CopyQ Homebrew cask** is deprecated (disabled 2026-09-01) because `CopyQ.app` is not signed for macOS Gatekeeper. Only the cask is affected — the upstream project is fine, and the Linux package is unaffected (see [hluk/CopyQ#3498](https://github.com/hluk/CopyQ/issues/3498)). Maccy is the most maintained signed-and-on-brew clipboard manager for macOS; the trade-off is no shipped CLI, so we query the plaintext SQLite at `~/Library/Application Support/Maccy/Storage.sqlite` (cask install) or `~/Library/Containers/org.p0deje.Maccy/.../Storage.sqlite` (Mac App Store sandboxed).

# Fix silent OSC 52 clipboard failure for large scrollback copies

## Context

User question: does herdr-plus's Quick Action "copy pane" cross the SSH boundary, or is it local-only? Investigation confirmed `dot_config/herdr/executable_pane-copy.sh` already delegates to the repo's own `x copy` (`dot_dotfiles/bin/executable_x`), which auto-selects pbcopy/wl-copy/xclip/xsel and falls back to OSC 52 over bare SSH — so the mechanism the user thought might be missing (`x`'s cross-platform/SSH copy) is already wired in. No new backend is needed.

While confirming this, the user reported a concrete symptom: over SSH, copying **scrollback** (`prefix+S` / "Copy pane: content (scrollback)", i.e. `pane-copy.sh content --source recent`) did not land in the local clipboard, while copying process info / coord / cwd / dir (all short payloads) worked fine.

Root cause, confirmed by reading `executable_x` and this repo's own docs (`docs/tools/clipboard.md:170`, which already documents that OSC 52 is terminal-size-limited — "iTerm2 caps at 1 MB, many others at 64-256 KB"):

- `osc52_copy()` (`dot_dotfiles/bin/executable_x:61-76`) base64-encodes the entire payload and writes it to `/dev/tty` in one `printf`, with **no size check, no chunking, no warning**.
- OSC 52 has no delivery acknowledgment — the `write(2)` to `/dev/tty` succeeds regardless of whether the terminal on the other end accepts or silently drops an oversized escape sequence.
- `pane-copy.sh`'s `copy()` → `x copy` → `osc52_copy()` chain therefore returns success (exit 0) even when the terminal dropped the payload, so `pane-copy.sh:143`'s `echo "copied $source content for $pane"` fires unconditionally.
- Full pane scrollback easily exceeds the smallest common terminal caps (64-256 KB); process-info/coord/cwd/dir payloads are a handful of lines and always stay well under any cap. This exactly matches the reported pattern.

Second question (git pull rebase): already resolved, no action needed — `pull.rebase = true` + `rebase.autoStash = true` are already set globally via `modify_dot_gitconfig.tmpl:42-45`.

Git pull tmp — that item is closed; nothing further to plan for it.

## Fix: make the OSC 52 size cap loud instead of silent

Add a payload-size guard to `osc52_copy()` in `dot_dotfiles/bin/executable_x` (the single shared clipboard backend — this fixes the failure mode for every consumer, not just herdr's `pane-copy.sh`). Follow the file's existing convention: other backends in `copy_backend()` print a specific `err "..."` and `exit 1` when the backend is available but execution fails (as opposed to `return 1`, which is reserved for "this backend isn't applicable here, try the next one").

\```sh
osc52_copy() {
    [[ -w /dev/tty ]] || return 1
    command -v base64 >/dev/null 2>&1 || return 1

    local data
    data="$(base64 | tr -d '\n')"
    [[ -n "$data" ]] || return 0

    local max_len="${X_OSC52_MAX_BYTES:-75000}"
    if (( ${#data} > max_len )); then
        err "OSC 52 payload too large (${#data} bytes, cap ${max_len}); most terminals silently drop larger OSC 52 sequences (64-256KB is common, iTerm2 ~1MB)"
        err "tip: copy a smaller selection, or raise the cap: X_OSC52_MAX_BYTES=<n> x copy ..."
        exit 1
    fi

    if [[ -n "${TMUX:-}" ]]; then
        ...
    else
        ...
    fi
}
\```

- Threshold defaults to `75000` (base64 chars) — comfortably above normal use (a paragraph, a stack trace, a visible pane screen) but below the smallest commonly-documented terminal cap, so it only trips for genuinely oversized payloads like full scrollback dumps.
- Overridable via `X_OSC52_MAX_BYTES` env var for users on terminals with a larger cap (e.g. iTerm2's ~1 MB).
- `exit 1` (not `return 1`) so `copy_backend()` does NOT also print the generic "no clipboard backend found" help text on top of this specific message — matches how `pbcopy`/`wl-copy`/`xclip`/`xsel` branches already behave on execution failure.
- Because `pane-copy.sh` runs under `set -eu` with no `pipefail`-masking here, `copy "$body"`'s new non-zero exit propagates and aborts the script **before** the misleading `echo "copied $source content for $pane"` line — the user now sees the real error instead of a false success message.

### Docs update (same commit)

`docs/tools/clipboard.md`:
- Add a row to the **Common failure modes** table (~line 155-164): large OSC 52 payload (e.g. full pane scrollback) silently dropped by the terminal → `x copy` now detects and reports this (as of this fix) instead of reporting false success; fix is to copy a smaller selection or raise `X_OSC52_MAX_BYTES`.
- Extend the **Design notes** bullet at line 170 to mention the new size guard and the `X_OSC52_MAX_BYTES` override.

No changes needed to `pane-copy.sh` itself — the fix in the shared `x copy` backend is sufficient; the error now propagates naturally through the existing `set -eu` + unguarded `copy "$body"` call.

## Verification

- `printf 'x%.0s' {1..100000} | x copy` (bash brace expansion) over a plain SSH session (no `DISPLAY`/`WAYLAND_DISPLAY`) — should now print the new `err` diagnostic and exit 1, not silently "succeed".
- `printf 'short text' | x copy` — should still succeed normally (regression check on the common case).
- `X_OSC52_MAX_BYTES=200000 printf 'x%.0s' {1..100000} | x copy` — should succeed once the cap is raised past the payload size.
- Over herdr + SSH: `prefix+S` (scrollback copy) on a pane with a large scrollback should now surface the error instead of a false "copied" message; on a pane with modest scrollback it should still copy successfully.

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-08-15 15:21:24Z)**_

## Summary

**Answer to your questions:**
1. **herdr-plus copy pane**: already cross-platform-safe — `pane-copy.sh` delegates to `x copy`, which auto-selects pbcopy/wl-copy/xclip/xsel and falls back to OSC 52 over bare SSH. The actual bug you hit (scrollback copy failing while process/coord/cwd/dir succeeded) was that OSC 52 has no payload size cap: full scrollback exceeds most terminals' silent-drop threshold (64–256KB), while the small payloads always succeed — and OSC 52 has no delivery ack, so `x copy` reported success even when the terminal dropped it.
2. **git pull rebase**: already configured (`pull.rebase=true` + `rebase.autoStash=true` globally via `modify_dot_gitconfig.tmpl`) — no change needed.

**Fix applied**: `dot_dotfiles/bin/executable_x`'s `osc52_copy()` now refuses payloads over 75000 base64 chars (override via `X_OSC52_MAX_BYTES`) with a clear error instead of silently writing a doomed escape sequence. Updated `docs/tools/clipboard.md`'s failure-modes table and design notes to match. Verified with shellcheck (clean) and manual tests confirming the guard fires on oversized payloads and is bypassable via the env var.

It distills a herdr CLI call into human-readable text and pipes it to the repo's own [`x copy`](../shells/aliases.md) (auto-selects pbcopy / wl-copy / xclip / xsel / OSC 52; `x` is resolved by absolute-path fallback since a command-pane may run without the interactive PATH). The pane defaults to the **current focused pane** (`herdr pane current`); the keybinds pass `$HERDR_ACTIVE_PANE_ID`, the Quick Actions pass `$HERDR_PLUS_PANE_ID`, and either falls through to the current-pane lookup when empty.
401	
402	| Op | Key | Quick Action | What lands on the clipboard |
403	|---|---|---|---|
404	| `process` | `prefix+P` | *Copy pane: process info* | foreground processes — `cmdline` + `pid` + `cwd` (from `herdr pane process-info`) |
405	| `coord` | `prefix+D` | *Copy pane: coordinate* | a paste-ready `session` / `workspace` / `tab` / `pane` id block + the `socket` path + a `# herdr pane get <pane>` line |
406	| `content` (visible) | `prefix+V` | *Copy pane: content (visible)* | the pane's on-screen text (`herdr pane read --source visible`) |
407	| `content` (scrollback) | `prefix+S` | *Copy pane: content (scrollback)* | the pane's full retained scrollback (`--source recent`) |
408	| `dir` | `prefix+d` | *Copy space: dir* | the **workspace ("space") root directory** — see below |
409	| `cwd` | `prefix+ctrl+d` | *Copy pane: cwd* | the focused pane's **live** working directory (what `pwd` / [`abspath`](../shells/aliases.md) returns) |
410	
411	The **coordinate** answers "which `session > space > tab > pane` is this?" in a form you can feed back to the CLI. herdr has **no `--session` flag** on the `pane`/`tab`/`workspace` subcommands — a session is targeted only via `HERDR_SOCKET_PATH` — so the block includes the `socket=` line as the session selector (the session *name* is resolved by matching that socket against `herdr session list --json`).
412	
413	Both surfaces share the same helper: the `[[keys.command]]` binds in [`.chezmoitemplates/herdr/config.toml`](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles/blob/main/.chezmoitemplates/herdr/config.toml) and the `copy-*.toml` **Quick Actions** under `dot_config/herdr/plugins/config/cloudmanic.herdr-plus/quick-actions/` (fuzzy-launched via `prefix+y`). `P/D/V/S` are uppercase (`prefix+shift+<letter>`) chosen to dodge herdr's reserved `shift+H/J/K/L` (swap-pane) and this repo's `shift+B` (new_worktree) / `shift+R` (reload); lowercase `d` was the only free mnemonic letter left for the dir ops, with `ctrl+d` keeping the pair adjacent. Confirm no collision with `herdr server reload-config` (empty `diagnostics`).
```

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-08-15 15:27:55Z)**_

## Root cause found and fixed

Your report was right and it wasn't the OSC 52 size cap — it was a separate, much simpler bug:

**`herdr pane read` defaults to only 80 lines** when `--lines` isn't passed. `pane-copy.sh`'s `content` case never passed `--lines`, so `prefix+S` / "Copy pane: content (scrollback)" was silently grabbing just the last 80 lines regardless of how much scrollback the pane actually retained (your `w8:p1W` pane has ~1891 lines retained per `max_offset_from_bottom`). I confirmed by probing `--lines` values directly: `500`→500 lines, `1000`→1000, `1900`/`2000`/`5000`→still capped at exactly 1000 — so **1000 lines is herdr's own hard per-call ceiling**, with no pagination flag to go further back.

**Fix applied** in `dot_config/herdr/executable_pane-copy.sh`: the `content` case now passes `--lines 1000` explicitly, so scrollback copies get herdr's actual maximum (12.5x more than before) instead of the accidental 80-line default. Updated the script's header comment and `docs/tools/herdr.md`'s copy-ops table to document the real 1000-line ceiling honestly (it's still not literally "full" scrollback for panes with >1000 retained lines — that's a herdr CLI limitation, not something this repo can page around).

The earlier OSC 52 size-guard fix is still valid and stays in — it protects against genuinely huge payloads (other panes, other tools using `x copy`) — but it wasn't what caused this particular report.

```text
3:[ogulcancelik/herdr](https://github.com/ogulcancelik/herdr) is a Rust terminal multiplexer with **built-in coding-agent awareness** (it tracks per-pane agent state: idle / working / blocked / done). It sits in the same niche as tmux/zellij but is mouse-first and agent-native. Docs: <https://herdr.dev/docs/>.
20:> The flow is **detach (`prefix+q`) → run it in a plain terminal → reattach with bare `herdr`**. Detaching does not kill anything (client close ≠ session loss), and `--handoff` then swaps the server without exiting pane processes — verified 2026-07 upgrading 0.7.1 → 0.7.5 with a Claude Code session running in a pane, which survived uninterrupted. `just upgrade-herdr` encodes this: it *skips with instructions* rather than failing when it detects `HERDR_ENV`/`HERDR_PANE_ID`, so `just upgrade-all` from a herdr pane doesn't die here. Full trace: [`pitfalls/herdr-update-handoff-refuses-inside-pane.md`](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles/blob/main/pitfalls/herdr-update-handoff-refuses-inside-pane.md).
27:> **Why a package-managed herdr strands its own server — the reason macOS left Homebrew.** herdr's socket API is protocol-versioned, and a package-manager upgrade cannot restart the server, so after `brew upgrade herdr` every CLI call (and therefore every `tv herdr-*` channel, `hvibe`/`hcode`, and `[[keys.command]]` helper) fails `protocol_mismatch` until the server restarts — which kills all pane processes. `herdr update --handoff`, the live pane-preserving path, is **disabled on Homebrew/mise/Nix installs**, so a brew-installed herdr has no way to avoid that restart. This repo now installs the self-managed release binary on macOS too, which is what closes the gap; the pitfall below is kept because it still describes what happens on any box that has not been migrated (and `just upgrade-herdr` skips with instructions when it detects a package-managed install). Check with `herdr status` (`compatible:` / `restart_needed:`), not `herdr --version`. Full recovery matrix: [`pitfalls/herdr-brew-upgrade-strands-running-server.md`](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles/blob/main/pitfalls/herdr-brew-upgrade-strands-running-server.md).
90:- **New tabs follow the focused pane's live cwd (herdr ≥0.7.x).** With `new_cwd = "follow"` (below), a *new tab* inherits the focused pane's live cwd — same as a *split*. herdr [issue #912](https://github.com/ogulcancelik/herdr/issues/912) changed `follow` so tabs behave like splits; the older "new tab opens at the workspace root (often `$HOME`)" was treated as a bug and removed. There is **no `new_cwd` value** (and no workspace-level cwd — `herdr workspace get` exposes none) that opens a new tab at the workspace root; for that use **`prefix+C`** (below).
122:| `sesh` fuzzy switch + `tmuxp` layouts | **Plugin** [herdr-plus](https://github.com/cloudmanic/herdr-plus) Projects + Quick Actions | Plugin + Projects templates |

229:[herdr-plus](https://github.com/cloudmanic/herdr-plus) adds **Projects** (declarative multi-tab/multi-pane workspace templates with a fuzzy picker — the `tmuxp`/`tmuxinator` analog) and **Quick Actions** (a fuzzy command launcher — the popup-menu analog).

It reads the pane (`herdr pane read`), runs the **same extraction/rewrite passes as tmux-fzf-url**, and opens each choice with the repo's cross-platform [`x open`](../shells/aliases.md) (wslview / open / xdg-open). It mirrors `pane-copy.sh` exactly: pane defaults to `$HERDR_ACTIVE_PANE_ID` (the keybind var) with a `herdr pane current` fallback, and `x` is resolved by absolute-path fallback since a command-pane may run without the interactive PATH.
449:Bound via a `[[keys.command]] type="pane"` in [`.chezmoitemplates/herdr/config.toml`](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles/blob/main/.chezmoitemplates/herdr/config.toml) — no tv channel needed (fzf is the faithful port). Copy-mode URL opening (tmux's `tmux-open` `o`) has no herdr equivalent; use `prefix+u` for the picker.
455:Helper: `~/.config/herdr/path-pick.sh` = [`dot_config/herdr/executable_path-pick.sh`](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles/blob/main/dot_config/herdr/executable_path-pick.sh), a direct sibling of `url-pick.sh`/`pane-copy.sh` (same pane + `x`-resolution + `herdr pane read` plumbing), copying via [`x copy`](../shells/aliases.md).
469:herdr has **no native usage/quota/token display** (the sidebar shows agent *state* only). It does expose a per-pane hook — `herdr pane report-metadata <pane> --source ID --token usage="…" --ttl-ms N` — that a driver could push a `"Claude 62% • Codex 78%"` label into (the same hook the **Review-pending flag** section above uses, but since herdr 0.7.4 tokens are a namespaced map, so a `usage` token and the `review` token coexist instead of contending for one field). A Codex-only community plugin ([jerryfane/herdr-codex-usage-kit](https://github.com/jerryfane/herdr-codex-usage-kit)) already does this from the same `~/.codex` data [CodexBar](https://github.com/steipete/CodexBar) reads; nothing covers Claude/ChatGPT quota. Deferred — CodexBar's menu bar stays the multi-provider view. Design + options captured in [`backlog/herdr-usage-status-driver.md`](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles/blob/main/backlog/herdr-usage-status-driver.md).

=== #1717 ===
pane.read returns truncated: false when the result is clearly truncated [CLOSED/COMPLETED]

### Is this a reproducible bug?

- [x] I confirm this is a reproducible bug, not a feature request, idea, question, contribution proposal, or direction check.

### Current behavior

`pane.read` (socket API) returns `read.truncated: false` even when the returned text is shorter than the requested `lines` and more content exists on the pane. The flag does not reflect whether the read was cut off.

### Expected behavior

`truncated` should be `true` whenever `pane.read` returned fewer lines than the pane has available above the returned window — i.e. when there is more content the caller did not receive. A `false` that means "there is more, I just didn't return it" is indistinguishable from "you have everything."

### Reproduction

Against the socket API, on a pane with more than 5 lines of content:

```
{"method":"pane.read","params":{"pane_id":"<id>","source":"recent","lines":5,"format":"text"}}
```

Returns 5 lines with `read.truncated: false`, despite further lines being present — a follow-up read with `lines: 5000` returns them. Observed on both a plain shell pane and a full-screen TUI pane.

### Impact

A client uses `truncated` to decide whether to offer a "load older" control for fetching earlier scrollback. Because the flag is always `false`, the control never appears, and the client cannot fetch beyond the first read window even when more content exists and is retrievable.

### Environment

- Herdr version: 0.7.4
- Update channel (stable or preview): stable
- Operating system: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS
- Terminal: xterm-256color
- Shell, if relevant: bash
- Relevant config, if any: none

pane.read cannot return a full-screen TUI pane's scrollback, only the current viewport [CLOSED/NOT_PLANNED]

### Is this a reproducible bug?

- [x] I confirm this is a reproducible bug, not a feature request, idea, question, contribution proposal, or direction check.

### Current behavior

For a pane running a full-screen TUI (an agent CLI, vim, less, htop), `pane.read --source recent --lines N` returns only about one viewport height regardless of `N`. The pane's earlier content — which is scrollable inside herdr's own TUI — cannot be retrieved through the socket API. A plain shell pane with equivalent output returns its real scrollback.

### Expected behavior

`pane.read` should be able to return a full-screen TUI pane's earlier content up to the requested `lines`, matching what herdr's TUI can already scroll back through — not just the current frame.

### Reproduction

```
seq 1 3000 | less
```

Page/jump through it, then over the socket API:

```
{"method":"pane.read","params":{"pane_id":"<id>","source":"recent","lines":5000,"format":"text"}}
```

Returns only ~33–70 lines, never the full 3000. The same read against a plain shell pane with 3000 lines of output returns them.

### Impact

A client built on `pane.read` (a browser/mobile terminal mirror) can only render what the API returns, so for a full-screen TUI it can only ever show one screen. Reading back a long agent session from such a client is impossible — the history is retained by herdr and visible in its TUI, but not reachable through the API.

### Environment

- Herdr version: 0.7.4
- Update channel (stable or preview): stable
- Operating system: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS
- Terminal: xterm-256color
- Shell, if relevant: bash
- Relevant config, if any: none

https://herdr.dev/docs/agent-automation/#known-caveat-alternate-screen-output

```text
`herdr pane read --lines 0` accepts the argument but returns empty output [CLOSED/NOT_PLANNED]


### Current behavior

`herdr pane read <pane> --lines 0` is accepted without an error and exits 0, but it prints nothing — zero bytes. Every other value of `--lines` reads content as expected; only `0` yields an empty result.

### Expected behavior

`--lines 0` should either be rejected as an invalid argument, or produce a sensible result. Silently returning empty output on exit 0 is surprising, because the caller cannot tell an empty pane apart from a swallowed argument.

### Reproduction

Pick any live pane from `herdr pane list`, then compare `--lines 0` against a positive value:

```
$ herdr pane read <pane> --lines 0 | wc -c
0
$ herdr pane read <pane> --lines 1 | wc -c
122
$ herdr pane read <pane> --lines 5 | wc -c
499
```

`--lines 0` returns 0 bytes (exit 0), while `--lines 1` and up return content.

### Impact

A script that computes a line count and passes `0` (an empty tail, an off-by-one, a `max(n-1, ...)` result) gets back empty output with a success exit code and no signal that the argument was the problem. That is easy to misread as "the pane is empty."

### Environment

- herdr version: 0.7.1
- OS: macOS 26.5.1 (build 25F80), arm64
- Update channel: unknown

# Documentation of `pane read` Lines Parameter

Based on the provided documentation, here's what is specified about the `lines` parameter:

**Default behavior:** "For recent sources, `--lines N` selects the last N rendered terminal rows before optional unwrapping; without it, reads default to 80 rows."

**For other source types:** "For `visible` and `detection`, omitting `--lines` returns the full snapshot, while specifying it keeps the last N newline-delimited lines."

**No documented maximum is mentioned.** The documentation does not specify any hard cap on the number of lines `pane read` can return per call. It only establishes that the default is 80 rows for recent sources and the full snapshot for visible/detection sources when `--lines` is omitted.

Based on the documentation provided, `herdr pane read` supports these flags:

- `--source` (values: `visible|recent|recent-unwrapped|detection`)
- `--lines N`
- `--format` (values: `text|ansi`)

_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-08-15 15:33:06Z)**_

Good findings — here's the full picture, sourced both from herdr's own docs and their GitHub issue tracker:

**1. Is `--lines` mandatory?**
Yes. herdr's own docs (herdr.dev/docs/agent-automation) state it plainly: *"For recent sources, `--lines N` selects the last N rendered terminal rows before optional unwrapping; **without it, reads default to 80 rows**."* So omitting `--lines` isn't an edge case — it's documented, intended behavior that just happens to be a bad default for "copy full scrollback."

**2. What if you need more than 1000?**
There's no way to get more via `pane read` today. I re-verified the ceiling: `--lines 500`→500, `1000`→1000, `1900`/`2000`/`5000`→always exactly 1000. `herdr pane read` has no offset/pagination flag, so anything beyond the most recent 1000 lines is currently unreachable through this command, full stop.

**3. Is the 1000 cap documented anywhere?**
No — checked herdr.dev's `agent-automation`, `socket-api`, and `cli-reference` docs pages directly, plus the local `herdr api schema` (which declares `lines` as `integer|null, minimum: 0` with **no `maximum`**). It's an undocumented, empirically-discovered server-side clamp.

**4. Any GitHub issue about it?**
Nothing filed specifically about this 1000-line ceiling, but I found closely related ones on `ogulcancelik/herdr`:
- [#1717](https://github.com/ogulcancelik/herdr/issues/1717) — *"`pane.read` returns `truncated: false` when the result is clearly truncated"* — confirmed and fixed, **released in v0.8.0**. Our installed version is **0.7.5**, so we don't have this yet. Even once fixed, that honest `truncated` flag only exists in the raw socket-API JSON response — I checked, `herdr pane read`'s CLI text/`--raw` output never surfaces it, so `pane-copy.sh` can't detect truncation that way without talking to the socket API directly (out of scope for a shell script).
- [#1718](https://github.com/ogulcancelik/herdr/issues/1718) — full-screen TUI panes losing scrollback beyond the viewport — closed `NOT_PLANNED`/"expected," but that's a different cause (alt-screen apps) and doesn't apply to your plain shell pane.
- [#1965](https://github.com/ogulcancelik/herdr/issues/1965) — "expose pane scrollback to socket-API clients" — closed, presumably what shipped as `pane.read` itself.

So: the 1000-line cap is real, currently unavoidable, and worth filing upstream if you want it addressed — I haven't opened anything since that's a public action I'd want your go-ahead on first. Want me to draft/file that issue?
